1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Ferrand Hale LLP is a fictional mid-size London law firm. Its Regulatory Investigations practice group had 24 associates on 1 October 2025. In the following twelve months nine of them resigned. In October 2025 a lateral partner, Dorian Faulk, joined the group, and the group won 'Kestrel', its largest matter so far: a regulator-ordered review for Halvergate Bank. The managing partner, the group head and the associates each explain the departures differently.
9	Your request: The management committee has postponed its decision and asked you to say what is driving the associate departures in Regulatory Investigations and what the firm should do next. Three interventions have been proposed, and the managing partner wants to announce a retention payment this month and close the review.
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Email from Graham Teversham, Managing Partner, to the management committee, 29 September 2026 (leadership-account): Colleagues — we have now lost nine associates from Regulatory Investigations in twelve months. I've spoken to two recruiters and the picture is clear: Brennick & Stowe are paying around £15k more at three years' qualification, and our people know it. Seven of the nine exit forms give 'career opportunity' as the reason, which in my experience means money. The January billable-target change applies to every group, so it can't explain one group. I propose a £12k retention payment for every associate in the group, announced this month, after which I'd like us to close this review and move on. — GT
12	- HR attrition report, 12 months to 30 September 2026 (system-record): Voluntary associate resignations, 1 Oct 2025 – 30 Sep 2026. Regulatory Investigations: 9 resignations against an opening headcount of 24 (37.5%); prior year 3 of 23 (13.0%). Other groups: Corporate 12.1% (prior year 13.4%); Banking 14.0% (12.8%); Disputes 11.5% (12.2%); Real Estate 13.3% (14.1%). Regulatory Investigations resignations by month: Dec 2025 (1), Feb 2026 (2), Mar (1), May (2), Jun (1), Aug (1), Sep (1). The firm-wide associate billable target rose from 1,900 to 2,000 hours from 1 January 2026, for all groups. This report does not record matter assignment or supervising partner.
13	- Memo from Priya Lindqvist, head of Regulatory Investigations, 2 October 2026 (manager-account): Two things changed in October 2025. Dorian Faulk joined us as a partner from another firm, and we won the Kestrel mandate, a regulator-ordered review of complaints handling for Halvergate Bank and the largest matter this group has run. At its peak Kestrel had 11 associates. The document-review phase runs to the end of December 2026. From January 2027 the matter moves to report drafting with four associates. Big investigations are hard on juniors; that is the nature of the work. Dorian brought Kestrel in and is exactly the partner this group needed. I would resist any account that makes this about him.
14	- Regulatory Investigations associate pulse survey, July 2026 (15 of 20 responded) (anonymous-staff-survey): Scores out of 5, with the firm-wide average in brackets: 'My workload is sustainable' 2.3 (3.4). 'The partners I work for treat me with respect' 2.8 (3.9). 'I get useful feedback on my work' 2.9 (3.6). 'I am fairly paid relative to the market' 3.0 (new item; no firm comparison). Selected free-text comments: 'Months of weekends on the investigation. Nobody can keep this up.' — 'Drafts come back after midnight with corrections copied to the whole team. It's humiliating.' — 'Rival firms pay more for less.' — 'I'd stay if I could get off the big matter.' The survey tool does not record which matters respondents work on.
15	- Management committee minutes, 6 October 2026 (extract) (document): Item 4, Regulatory Investigations attrition. The committee agreed to postpone a decision until the analysis is done. Options tabled: (a) a £12k retention payment for every associate in the group (GT), estimated cost £228k across 19 associates; (b) contract reviewers to take over Kestrel first-level review, about £160k absorbed by the firm because the client will not fund it (PL); (c) moving supervision of Kestrel associates to another partner (associate representative). HR reported that an external interviewer could hold confidential interviews with departed and current associates within three weeks for about £9k. Four of the nine leavers have already agreed to take part. Action: analyst to recommend.
16	
17	BRIEF:
18	Resignations are concentrated in the Kestrel team: 8 of 11 Kestrel associates left, against 1 of 13 other associates in the group. Other groups look normal, and the billable-target rise applied firm-wide, so neither it nor general market mobility explains this. Pay is probably not the main driver, since the Kestrel/non-Kestrel split is so lopsided, though pay may play a smaller part. I can't yet separate the heavy Kestrel workload from Dorian Faulk's supervision: all 11 Kestrel associates reported to him and he supervises no one else. The survey comments point to both. The exit forms are weak evidence because leavers knew the group head might read them. I'd advise against the £12k group-wide payment and closing the review. It would not address the concentration and would end the inquiry. Commission the confidential external interviews (about £9k, three weeks), structured to separate workload from supervision. Meanwhile, add matter and supervising partner to attrition reporting. Hold off on moving supervision or funding contract reviewers until the interviews show which cause matters. Confidence in the concentration finding is high. Confidence on supervision versus workload is low.
19
